Practical Scaling Laws:
Converting Compute into Performance in a Data-Constrained World

Christopher M. Bryant Affiliation: Arena Physica Email: chris@arenaphysica.com    Hao Liu Affiliation: Arena Physica Email: hao@arenaphysica.com
Abstract

The scaling laws guiding modern model training were calibrated for a single regime: data-rich, single-epoch pretraining. The dominant such scaling law form, Chinchilla’s L=E+A/Nα+B/DβL=E+A/N^{\alpha}+B/D^{\beta}, has three structural limitations outside that regime: it diverges as unique data shrinks instead of saturating at the uninformed baseline; it cannot represent overfitting when capacity exceeds the data; and it conflates total examples seen with unique examples available. We propose a closed-form extension, L⁡(N,D,T)=E+(L0−E)​h/(1+h)L(N,D,T)=E+(L_{0}-E)\,h/(1+h) with h=a/Nα+b/Tβ+c​Nγ/Dδh=a/N^{\alpha}+b/T^{\beta}+c\,N^{\gamma}/D^{\delta}, that decomposes loss into undercapacity, undertraining, and overfitting terms. It saturates between the irreducible loss EE and an uninformed baseline L0L_{0} fixed by the loss type, and reduces to Chinchilla in the data-rich, single-epoch limit. We validate it on four multi-epoch experiments spanning four architecture families (MLPs, ResNets, Fourier neural operators, and transformers) across vision, scientific ML, and language domains, and refit it to five published LLM scaling-law grids. Extrapolating to higher compute and larger unique data than seen at fit time, our form achieves state-of-the-art RMSE on every published LLM grid we evaluate and on most cells of our constructed experiments. Once calibrated, the form admits a cost-aware allocation that recovers Chinchilla’s optimum when data is free and shifts toward smaller corpora and more epochs as data grows expensive.

1 Introduction

For most modern ML, training data is expensive. Physics surrogates require running an expensive PDE solver to generate each example [2]; medical-imaging foundation models require expert-labeled data [25]; reinforcement-learning agents pay for every transition [39]; LLM finetuning operates at fractions of pretraining data budgets [50]. Even frontier LLM pretraining, where data has historically been the cheap input relative to compute, is starting to revisit tokens as scraped text runs out [47, 37]. In all of these settings, the practitioner faces the same tradeoff: spend dollars to acquire more unique data, or spend compute to revisit the data already in hand. Reasoning about that tradeoff is what scaling laws are for, but the dominant scaling law was calibrated in a regime where the tradeoff did not exist.

Scaling laws fit a parametric model of the loss surface from cheap small-scale runs and use it to predict loss at scales practitioners cannot afford to run. The most-cited instance is the Chinchilla form [24]:

L⁡(N,D)=E+ANα+BDβ.L(N,D)=E+\frac{A}{N^{\alpha}}+\frac{B}{D^{\beta}}. (1)

Variants of this power-law-plus-constant template recur across language modeling [26], vision [1], transfer learning [22], downstream tasks [10, 14], and theoretical models [3, 35, 8], and inherit its structural commitments.

Three structural failures.

Though Equation (1) and its close relatives have been used to fit training runs across many orders of magnitude in the data-rich, single-epoch regime, these forms lack three crucial properties needed to generalize beyond this regime:

  • •

    No baseline saturation. The loss should be bounded above by L0L_{0}, the loss of a model that has not learned anything. Chinchilla has L→∞L\to\infty as D→0D\to 0 instead of saturating at L0L_{0}.

  • •

    Overfitting unreachable. At fixed DD, the form is strictly decreasing in NN, but neural networks with N≫DN\gg D overfit [21, 37]: validation loss can rise with capacity past a point.

  • •

    No compute axis independent of (N,D)(N,D). The form cannot distinguish between total examples seen TT and unique examples DD, precluding the analysis of multi-epoch training runs.

The paper’s contributions are:

  • •

    A single parametric form for L⁡(N,D,T)L(N,D,T) on ℝ>03\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{3} that addresses these failures by decomposing loss into undercapacity, undertraining, and overfitting terms wrapped in a saturating bound between the irreducible loss EE and an uninformed baseline L0L_{0} (Section 2).

  • •

    A set of scaling experiments testing the form across four architecture-domain pairs that span vision, scientific machine learning, and language.

  • •

    An empirical demonstration of state-of-the-art extrapolation capabilities across prior published LLM scaling-law datasets.

  • •

    A strategy that chooses (N∗,D∗,T∗)(N^{*},D^{*},T^{*}) to minimize loss given a budget constraint, while optimally allocating that budget between data acquisition and training compute.

2 The extended scaling law

Motivated by the boundary failures of Equation (1), we enumerate a list of limiting behaviors (Table 1) that any form in (N,D,T)(N,D,T) should exhibit when NN, DD, or TT goes to either 00 or ∞\infty. Rows 1–5 require L→L0L\to L_{0} when training collapses and row 6 characterizes optimal behavior.

Proposed form.

We seek a simple closed-form extension of the Chinchilla functional form that obeys the desired limiting behaviors, decomposes into terms with clear physical meaning, and reduces to Equation (1) in the small-hh single-epoch limit. Working from those constraints, we arrive at the following form (full derivations are in Appendix A):

L⁡(N,D,T)=E+(L0−E)⋅h⁡(N,D,T)1+h⁡(N,D,T),h=aNα+bTβ+c​NγDδ.L(N,D,T)=E+(L_{0}-E)\cdot\frac{h(N,D,T)}{1+h(N,D,T)},\qquad h=\frac{a}{N^{\alpha}}+\frac{b}{T^{\beta}}+c\,\frac{N^{\gamma}}{D^{\delta}}. (2)

Notation.

NN is parameters, DD unique training examples, TT total training examples seen (counted with repetition). The three terms in hh represent undercapacity (a/Nαa/N^{\alpha}), undertraining (b/Tβb/T^{\beta}), and overfitting (c​Nγ/Dδc\,N^{\gamma}/D^{\delta}); the saturating wrapper h/(1+h)h/(1+h) bounds LL in [E,L0][E,L_{0}], where EE is the irreducible loss and L0L_{0} is the uninformed baseline loss. When necessary for analysis, compute CC is approximated as C≈k​N​TC\approx kNT with architecture-dependent constant kk (though the form makes no assumption about the functional relationship between CC, NN, and TT), and T/DT/D is the number of training epochs. The eight free parameters are (E,a,b,c,α,β,γ,δ)(E,a,b,c,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta).

What LL represents.

Throughout, L⁡(N,D,T)L(N,D,T) is the lowest validation loss seen during training: the minimum over checkpoints, not the final-checkpoint value. The convention matters in the overfitting regime (N≫DN\gg D), where validation loss can rise as the model memorizes; we fit to the achievable minimum, which is what a real deployment would early-stop at.

Scope of a fit.

A single fit of LL is conditional on a fixed architecture family, training-set distribution, and training recipe (optimizer, LR schedule, regularization, batch size, hyperparameter-selection protocol). These choices reshape the loss surface and are absorbed into the fitted constants.

2.1 Three decomposed terms

The difficulty hh is a sum of power laws that represent three distinct underperformance phenomena:

h⁡(N,D,T)=aNα⏟undercapacity+bTβ⏟undertraining+c​NγDδ⏟overfitting.h(N,D,T)=\underbrace{\frac{a}{N^{\alpha}}}_{\text{undercapacity}}+\underbrace{\frac{b}{T^{\beta}}}_{\text{undertraining}}+\underbrace{c\,\frac{N^{\gamma}}{D^{\delta}}}_{\text{overfitting}}. (3)

Undercapacity a/Nαa/N^{\alpha} is the only term that does not vanish as DD and TT grow without bound. It captures the residual cost of a model with finite capacity, and its exponent α\alpha is the standard Chinchilla capacity exponent. The precise way that NN maps to capacity depends on the model architecture, but within a given architecture, capacity increases monotonically with NN.

Undertraining b/Tβb/T^{\beta} decays with the total examples seen TT. In practice, TT is often taken as ≈C/(k​N)\approx C/(kN) with kk architecture-dependent, but the form does not require any strict relationship between CC and TT. Per Chinchilla single-epoch fits, β\beta is the data-axis exponent: at T=DT=D, b/Tβb/T^{\beta} collapses to b/Dβb/D^{\beta} and recovers the Chinchilla data term. Outside the single-epoch grid the two mechanisms separate: undertraining decays in TT regardless of whether each gradient step sees a fresh example or a repeat.

Overfitting c​Nγ/Dδc\,N^{\gamma}/D^{\delta} depends only on capacity NN and unique-data count DD, not on training duration. The two-exponent shape is more flexible than the symmetric ratio (N/D)γ(N/D)^{\gamma}: it allows DD-scaling and NN-scaling to be calibrated independently, since they enter generalization through different mechanisms (sample-size variance of the empirical-risk minimizer in DD, and capacity-driven excess representation in NN), each with its own scaling rate.

At fixed DD, the interplay between the overfitting term c​Nγ/DδcN^{\gamma}/D^{\delta} and undercapacity term a/Nαa/N^{\alpha} produces an interior minimum in L⁡(N)L(N) in the limit as T→∞T\to\infty (Appendix F.1), which implies that for a finite data size, there is a model size beyond which the best achievable performance not only saturates, but degrades. This U-shaped behavior is a structural feature absent from the other parametric forms surveyed in Section 5. We provide additional remarks on the relationship between “undercapacity” and “overfitting” in Appendix A.5.

2.2 The saturating wrapper

The wrapper h/(1+h)h/(1+h) is a monotone bijection from [0,∞)[0,\infty) to [0,1)[0,1) with two properties we want:

  1. 1.

    Small-hh linearity. For h≪1h\ll 1, h/(1+h)=h−h2+h3−⋯h/(1+h)=h-h^{2}+h^{3}-\cdots, so Equation (2) reduces at leading order to L≈E+(L0−E)​hL\approx E+(L_{0}-E)h. This is the regime in which Chinchilla was fit, and our form becomes Chinchilla-like there: the (L0−E)(L_{0}-E) prefactor is absorbed into the fitted coefficients of the power-law terms in hh.

  2. 2.

    Large-hh saturation. For h→∞h\to\infty, h/(1+h)→1h/(1+h)\to 1 and L→L0L\to L_{0}. The form cannot exceed the baseline.

Other wrappers satisfy the same endpoints; we compare against the natural alternative 1−e−h1-e^{-h} in Appendix A.4.

2.3 The baseline loss L0L_{0}

L0L_{0} is the loss of an uninformed baseline: a model that extracts no information from the data. It is determined by the loss type and the output normalization, not fitted to the loss surface. For cross-entropy over KK possible outcomes, L0=ln⁡KL_{0}=\ln K (Appendix A.1): K=VK=V for next-token prediction over a vocabulary of size VV, and KK is the number of classes for classification. For relative-L2L_{2} regression on zz-normalized targets, L0=1L_{0}=1 exactly, since zero predictions give ‖0−u‖2/‖u‖2=1\|0-u\|_{2}/\|u\|_{2}=1. For other bounded losses, L0L_{0} is the corresponding uninformed-baseline limit. We use L0L_{0} as a structural upper bound on the loss surface; per-dataset values are listed in Section 3.1.

2.4 Qualitative behavior

To gain intuition for the form, in Figure 1, we contrast our loss surface with Chinchilla’s. At a low, medium, and high value of DD, we plot two complementary views: isoFLOP curves L⁡(N∣C)L(N\mid C) at fixed compute, and training trajectories L⁡(C∣N)L(C\mid N) at fixed model size.

IsoFLOP curves L⁡(N∣C)L(N\mid C). Chinchilla’s isoFLOPs are U-shaped: they diverge to infinity on both tails and bottom out at a single minimum that defines the compute-optimal model size for that budget. As CC grows, this minimum shifts rightward toward larger model sizes and its loss approaches the irreducible floor EE. Our form’s isoFLOPs share that U-shape near the optimum, but differ at both extremes. The tails of our isoFLOPs saturate above at L0L_{0}, and for any finite DD they approach a different minimum loss value Eeff>EE_{\text{eff}}>E at a critical model size N∗N^{*}. Beyond that model size, the best achievable loss increases, even with infinite compute. As DD grows, N∗N^{*} shifts rightward and EeffE_{\text{eff}} descends toward EE. In the infinite-data-and-compute limit away from L0L_{0}, the envelope of our isoFLOPs coincides with Chinchilla’s.

Training trajectories L⁡(C∣N)L(C\mid N). By holding NN fixed instead, we can watch the loss evolve as compute increases. Chinchilla’s trajectories begin at infinity and decay monotonically: smaller models drop faster early on but settle at higher plateaus than larger ones. Ours instead begin at the finite ceiling L0L_{0} and likewise decay to an asymptote, but as NN grows, that asymptote first falls, reaching its minimum EeffE_{\text{eff}} at N=N∗N=N^{*}, then rises again.

3 Experiments

We empirically validate our proposed form by comparing it to prior forms across a variety of different calibration sets of (N,D,T)(N,D,T) points. We evaluate extrapolation performance on held-out high-CC or high-DD runs since extrapolation to these unseen regimes is the primary practical use of a scaling law. Our validation consists of two distinct sets of experiments:

Multi-domain, multi-epoch experiments (Appendix D).

First, we train four different families of model architectures in four different domains and control the full (N,D,T)(N,D,T) sweep, spanning a regime and design space largely unexplored by prior scaling-law work: MLPs on MNIST (10-way image classification: a toy problem where every limiting behavior is cheap to access; Figure 2), PreActResNets [18] on CIFAR-100 (100-way image classification), Fourier Neural Operators on PDEBench 2D Darcy flow [33, 45] (physical PDE simulation), and decoder-only transformers on TinyStories [13] (next-token prediction). In each of these domains, we fit our proposed form to the loss surface to evaluate the quality of the fit and the extrapolation error of the form, demonstrating its broad applicability. Full experimental details are in Appendix D.

Refits to prior LLM scaling studies (Appendix E).

Second, since the majority of prior scaling-law work focuses on language modeling with transformer architectures [26, 24, 37, 14, 31], we refit our form to five published LLM scaling-law grids, each chosen to probe a qualitatively different regime: Chinchilla [24] as the canonical compute-optimal reference; Muennighoff [37] for multi-epoch repetition (the only public grid with T>DT>D); Gadre [14] for the over-trained regime (D/ND/N up to ∼640\sim\!640); Porian [41] as a Kaplan stand-in (Kaplan’s raw data is not public; Porian re-runs Chinchilla-style training under a Kaplan-style LR schedule on RefinedWeb); and Farseer [31] as the largest open single-recipe grid at modern scale. Dataset and grid descriptions are in Appendix E.

3.1 Setup

Forms compared.

On each dataset, we evaluate our proposed form (Equation (2)) against five refitted parametric scaling law baselines: Chinchilla [24] (the canonical additive E+A/Nα+B/DβE+A/N^{\alpha}+B/D^{\beta} form), Muennighoff [37] (extends Chinchilla to multi-epoch via an exponentially-saturating effective-data substitution D→D′D\to D^{\prime}), M4 [1] (single-axis implicit form bounding LL in [E,L0][E,L_{0}]; closest structural analog of our wrapper), BNSL [10] (3+3​k3{+}3k-parameter smoothly-broken power-law in a composite scalar; the only baseline able to fit non-monotone L⁡(N)L(N), via kk empirical breakpoints), and Farseer [31] (L⁡(N,D)L(N,D) form with NN-dependent exponents; reports state-of-the-art far-compute extrapolation, which we reproduce in Appendix H). Appendix B lists each form’s equation, motivation, and free parameters. We also evaluate four ablations of our form in Appendix I.1: dropping the saturating wrapper, dropping the overfitting term, swapping h/(1+h)h/(1+h) for 1−e−h1{-}e^{-h}, and replacing the two-exponent overfitting term c​Nγ/Dδc\,N^{\gamma}/D^{\delta} with a single-exponent ratio c​(N/D)γc\,(N/D)^{\gamma}.

Baseline loss values.

Following the loss-type rule of Section 2, we fix L0L_{0} per dataset: ln⁡10≈2.30\ln 10\approx 2.30 for MNIST and ln⁡100≈4.61\ln 100\approx 4.61 for CIFAR-100 (classification), L0=1L_{0}=1 for Darcy (relative-L2L_{2} on zz-normalized targets), ln⁡2000≈7.60\ln 2000\approx 7.60 for TinyStories (our custom 2K BPE tokenizer trained on the TinyStories corpus), and for the public LLM grids ln⁡32,000≈10.37\ln 32{,}000\approx 10.37 (Chinchilla, Porian; SentencePiece), ln⁡50,257≈10.82\ln 50{,}257\approx 10.82 (Muennighoff; GPT-NeoX/GPT-2 vocabulary), ln⁡50,432≈10.83\ln 50{,}432\approx 10.83 (Gadre), and log2⁡(65,536)/4=4.0\log_{2}(65{,}536)/4=4.0 for Farseer, whose grid we score in bits per character rather than nats, to match the statistic its authors report.

Training recipe.

The form’s fitted constants are recipe-dependent (Section 2), so we assume a single training recipe within each experiment family and report exponents and coefficients conditional on that recipe. For three of our four training experiments, following Hägele et al. [15], we adopt a Warmup-Stable-Decay (WSD) schedule with brief cooldown forks at log-spaced compute targets, so a single stable run feeds multiple final-loss measurements at different total-compute budgets. We train our MNIST models with no LR schedule at all, so every step is a valid end state and no cooldown forks are needed. Per-family optimizer, LR, batch size, and warmup choices are in Appendix D. For the five published LLM grids we filter each source down to a single training recipe before fitting; per-grid filter rules are in Appendix E.

Form fitting.

Each form’s free parameters are fit by minimizing Huber loss on log-residuals with BFGS, with L0L_{0} fixed by the loss type and multistart random initializations to mitigate local optima (Appendix C.1). Full details are in Appendix C.

Extrapolation protocols.

Both holdouts target ∼\sim10% of rows, constructed groupwise on the relevant axis so no axis value is split across folds. high-CC holdout (predicting expensive runs from cheap ones): groupwise on CC, effectively the largest-CC 10% of rows since CC is near-continuous. high-DD holdout (predicting large-DD performance from small-DD data): groupwise on DD; since DD is highly discrete, the realized holdout is the top-DD group for all four of our experiments (ranging from 8% to 20%).

Evaluation.

We report the root-mean-square residual in log loss over the MM held-out rows,

RMSElog=1M​∑i=1M(ln⁡L^i−ln⁡Li)2,\mathrm{RMSE}_{\log}\;=\;\sqrt{\frac{1}{M}\sum\nolimits_{i=1}^{M}\big(\ln\hat{L}_{i}-\ln L_{i}\big)^{2}}, (4)

where LiL_{i} is row ii’s observed loss and L^i\hat{L}_{i} the fitted form’s prediction. Every reported interval is the 2.5%–97.5% quantile range over 200 bootstrap resamples of the training set, each refit from scratch. When comparing two forms directly to each other, we report a paired win-rate: draw a bootstrap resample of the training set, fit the two forms to it, note which form has the lower RMSE, repeat 200 times, and report the fraction of times the first form has the lower RMSE. Where a win-rate is called significant, the pp-value comes from an exact two-sided sign test of the win count against Bin⁡(200,12)\mathrm{Bin}(200,\tfrac{1}{2}).

3.2 Results

Figure 2 shows MNIST training run validation loss curves as a function of training FLOPs (averaged across 10 random seeds to reduce noise), split by NN and DD. These curves exhibit the qualitative behavior we anticipate in Section 2.4, consistent with the shape predicted by the proposed form. Table 2 reports held-out RMSE in log space across all forms under the high-CC and high-DD protocols defined above. Table 3 reports the paired win-rates of our form compared to each of the other forms. For completeness, we provide an ablation of all parts of our form, as well as random 5-fold cross-validation and in-sample metrics, in Appendix I.1.

Summary.

Our form has the lowest median held-out RMSE in 16 of the 18 high-CC and high-DD cells, ahead of the best competing baseline in those cells by a median factor of 1.5×1.5\times. Ours is also ahead of the best competing baseline in a majority of paired resamples in those same 16 cells, with wins that are all significant on a two-sided sign test at p<10−3p<10^{-3}. In addition, our form has the best predictive performance on the Farseer far-extrapolation task (detailed in Appendix H). The only two cells where our form underperforms a baseline are TinyStories high-CC and MNIST high-DD.

Take-away.

Our results confirm that our form performs well in the multi-epoch data-constrained regimes the form was designed for, when compared to other forms. Furthermore, its benefits are not confined to these regimes: it significantly outperforms all other forms when evaluated on traditional large-scale LLM scaling prediction tasks, indicating that it can be used as a general-purpose scaling law for LLMs. The underperformance on two cells from our experiments motivates the practical need to quantify the loss prediction uncertainty of any fitted form, so we detail a conformal prediction approach in Appendix G.

3.3 Compute footprint

All training ran on AWS Batch with one NVIDIA A10G GPU per job (g5.2xlarge). The campaign consumed ∼\sim206 GPU-hours total: MNIST ∼\sim46, CIFAR-100 ∼\sim14, Darcy ∼\sim48, and TinyStories ∼\sim98. Aggregate measured training compute is ∼\sim6.0×10186.0\times 10^{18} FLOPs, dominated by TinyStories (4.8×10184.8\times 10^{18}).

4 Cost-aware allocation

Beyond fitting held-out loss, a calibrated L⁡(N,D,T)L(N,D,T) answers two reciprocal questions of training economics. At unit prices ρD\rho_{D} per unique example and ρC\rho_{C} per FLOP, with total spend ℬ⁡(N,D,T)=ρD​D+ρC​k​N​T\mathcal{B}(N,D,T)=\rho_{D}D+\rho_{C}kNT: what is the minimum cost required to reach a target loss L∗L^{*}, and what is the minimum loss achievable within a fixed budget ℬmax\mathcal{B}_{\text{max}}? Under our form, both hh and ℬ\mathcal{B} are convex in (log⁡N,log⁡D,log⁡T)(\log N,\log D,\log T) (each is a sum of exponentials of affine functions), so both are convex programs with a unique optimum on a single Pareto frontier {(ℬ∗,L∗)}\{(\mathcal{B}^{*},L^{*})\}. The Lagrange first-order condition for the budget-constrained problem is

∂L/∂NρC​k​T=∂L/∂DρD=∂L/∂TρC​k​N,\frac{\partial L/\partial N}{\rho_{C}kT}\;=\;\frac{\partial L/\partial D}{\rho_{D}}\;=\;\frac{\partial L/\partial T}{\rho_{C}kN}, (5)

i.e., at the optimum the marginal loss reduction per dollar is equal across all three axes. The target-loss problem inverts these ratios and shares the same optimal allocation (N∗,D∗,T∗)(N^{*},D^{*},T^{*}). Appendix F.2 gives the full derivation and a numerical recipe.

Asymptotic regimes.

The dollar-cost ratio η=ρD/ρC\eta=\rho_{D}/\rho_{C} traces a continuum between two limits. When data is free (η→0\eta\to 0), the overfitting term vanishes and (N∗,T∗)(N^{*},T^{*}) reduces to Chinchilla compute-optimal, with our TT-axis playing the role of Chinchilla’s DD-axis. When data is expensive (each example a simulator run, paid label, or licensed token), the overfitting term binds and the optimum walks toward smaller DD, more epochs, and a smaller N∗N^{*}. Prior cost-aware analyses [43, 2, 4] inherit a Chinchilla-style loss with no overfitting term, leaving this data-expensive corner unrepresented.

Illustrative example.

At fixed total budget, we solve for the minimum-loss allocation on Chinchilla’s fitted exponents (α,β)=(0.34,0.28)(\alpha,\beta)=(0.34,0.28) [24] and illustrative overfitting constants (c,γ,δ)=(2×103,0.5,1.0)(c,\gamma,\delta)=(2\times 10^{3},0.5,1.0) chosen so the overfitting term binds at LLM-scale (N,D)(N,D) (Table 4). Increasing η\eta by 1000×1000\times from web-token economics to expert-label economics shrinks D∗D^{*} by two orders of magnitude, shrinks N∗N^{*} by ∼20×\sim 20\times, walks T∗/D∗T^{*}/D^{*} from ∼\sim3 to ∼1,250\sim 1{,}250 epochs, and shifts the optimal data-budget share from 12% to 86%.

5 Related work

Parametric scaling laws and Chinchilla extensions.

Power-law generalization curves [23, 42, 20] were unified into a joint L⁡(N,D)L(N,D) by Kaplan et al. [26], whose Equation 1.5 implies an overfitting ratio of N0.74/DN^{0.74}/D structurally close to our Nγ/DδN^{\gamma}/D^{\delta} term, but bundled inside a non-separable power so the NN- and DD-axis exponents cannot be fit independently. Hoffmann et al. [24] simplified this to the additive Equation (1) we recover as a small-hh limit. Subsequent work refines the protocol around Chinchilla’s form without changing its structural commitments: Gadre et al. [14] reparameterize via the token multiplier M=D/NM=D/N for over-trained models, Porian et al. [41] and Pearce and Song [40] re-examine fits under tighter optimization control, Besiroglu et al. [7] flag numerical issues in the original fits, Kumar et al. [28] layer a precision axis, Sardana et al. [43] add an inference-FLOPs term to the cost objective, and Hernandez et al. [22] introduce an effective-data notion under transfer. Li et al. [31] introduce Farseer, a 9-parameter L⁡(N,D)L(N,D) form with NN-dependent exponents reporting large extrapolation-error reductions over Chinchilla. None of these forms includes an explicit baseline L0L_{0} or a training-duration axis independent of (N,D)(N,D).

Saturating and non-monotone forms.

A line of work moves beyond the pure power-law-plus-constant template by introducing saturation. Muennighoff et al. [37] extend Chinchilla to multi-epoch training by replacing DD with an effective-data quantity that saturates exponentially in repetitions (and analogously NN with a saturating capacity quantity); Liew and Kato [34] document related saturation in continual pretraining. This treats TT via a fixed exponential curve in the data axis rather than as an independent power-law axis with its own exponent. Alabdulmohsin et al. [1]’s M4 family instead saturates in the loss axis, bounding LL between EE and L0L_{0} as our wrapper does, but is single-axis (one scalar xx rather than a joint h⁡(N,D,T)h(N,D,T)) and stated implicitly in LL. Caballero et al. [10]’s Broken Neural Scaling Laws (BNSL), a 3+3​k3{+}3k-parameter smoothly-broken power-law, can express saturation, inflection, and double descent via empirical breakpoints; standard practice fits BNSL with a composite scalar x⁡(N,D,C)x(N,D,C), yielding a single curve in xx rather than an (N,D,T)(N,D,T) decomposition, and bounding LL in [E,L0][E,L_{0}] only approximately. To our knowledge, the Nγ/DδN^{\gamma}/D^{\delta} term wrapped in h/(1+h)h/(1+h) is the first explicit closed-form overfitting term in this literature. Surveys [32, 12] catalog further variants; Appendix B collects the equation, motivation, and parameter count of every form we compare against.

Theory and other domains.

Theoretical analyses derive scaling exponents from first principles via random-feature, kernel, and dynamical models [35, 3, 8, 9]; these target the undercapacity and undertraining exponents and predict no overfitting term of our form. Parametric scaling outside language [49, 44, 39, 25] typically reuses or lightly adapts the LLM template and inherits its structural limitations.

6 Limitations

In-distribution validation loss only.

As in most of the scaling-law literature, our form predicts in-distribution validation loss (loss measured on held-out samples drawn from the same distribution as the training data). Downstream task performance scaling [14], task-level metrics, emergent capabilities, and out-of-distribution behavior are separate layers in the scaling-law stack and out of scope.

Double descent.

Classical double descent [6, 38] studies what happens at the interpolation threshold N≈DN\approx D rather than asymptotically far from it: test error spikes at the threshold and falls again past it, and theoretical results in linear regression and random features [5, 16, 36] characterize when interpolation is benign. Our form is asymptotic and smooth, so it does not predict a peak at N≈DN\approx D and does not attempt to capture this structure. We also do not observe the phenomenon in our experiments, likely because tracking best-so-far validation loss suppresses the model-wise peak [19, 38] and the peak’s typically narrow NN range falls between cells on our log-spaced grids.

Universality of fits.

While our form is generally applicable across architectures and domains, the fitted constants (E,a,b,c,α,β,γ,δ)(E,a,b,c,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta) are not. Several choices made before fitting are absorbed into these constants and can shift values materially across settings: the parameter-counting convention for NN, architecture family, and the training recipe (optimizer, schedule, regularization). A scaling law that unifies a fitted form across these choices is beyond the scope of this paper. Practitioners refitting our form should hold these choices fixed across the calibration grid and recalibrate per setting.

7 Conclusion

We introduced a closed-form scaling law L⁡(N,D,T)=E+(L0−E)​h/(1+h)L(N,D,T)=E+(L_{0}-E)\,h/(1+h) that decomposes loss into undercapacity, undertraining, and overfitting terms, bounded between the irreducible loss EE and an uninformed baseline L0L_{0} fixed by the loss type. The form satisfies six target limiting behaviors, five of which Chinchilla violates, reduces to Chinchilla in the data-rich single-epoch limit, and includes an explicit closed-form overfitting term c​Nγ/Dδc\,N^{\gamma}/D^{\delta} with no analog in prior parametric scaling laws. Across nine calibration grids spanning four architecture families and three domains, it wins 16 of 18 high-CC and high-DD extrapolation cells, with state-of-the-art held-out RMSE on every published LLM grid.

A calibrated L⁡(N,D,T)L(N,D,T) converts a single price ratio η=ρD/ρC\eta=\rho_{D}/\rho_{C} into a concrete cost-optimal allocation (N∗,D∗,T∗)(N^{*},D^{*},T^{*}): the data-free limit recovers Chinchilla compute-optimal, and as data grows expensive (a simulator run, an expert label, a licensed token), the allocation walks toward smaller corpora, more epochs, and smaller models, reaching budget shares prior cost-aware analyses (which inherit Chinchilla’s loss form) cannot describe.

We expect the structural ingredients introduced here (baseline saturation, an independent training-duration axis, and an explicit overfitting term) to inform new parametric scaling laws as practitioners move further into the compute-rich, data-constrained regime that motivates this work.

Appendix A Our proposed form

A.1 The uninformed baseline L0L_{0}

We derive the value L0=ln⁡VL_{0}=\ln V used in Equation (2) as the cross-entropy loss of an uninformed baseline: a model that extracts no information from the data and outputs a uniform distribution over the VV possible next tokens (analogously, L0=ln⁡KL_{0}=\ln K for KK-way classification).

Setup.

Let the data distribution be p⁡(x,y)p(x,y) over (context, next-token) pairs (x,y)(x,y) with y∈{1,…,V}y\in\{1,\ldots,V\}. The cross-entropy loss of a model q(⋅∣x)q(\cdot\mid x) is

L⁡(q)=𝔼(x,y)∼p​[−log⁡q⁡(y∣x)].L(q)\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim p}\bigl[-\log q(y\mid x)\bigr].

Uninformed baseline.

Define the uninformed baseline q0q_{0} by q0​(y∣x)=1/Vq_{0}(y\mid x)=1/V for all yy and all xx (the uniform output is the maximum-entropy distribution given no information about the input). Substituting,

L0≡L⁡(q0)=𝔼(x,y)∼p​[−log⁡(1/V)]=log⁡V,L_{0}\;\equiv\;L(q_{0})\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim p}\bigl[-\log(1/V)\bigr]\;=\;\log V,

where the last equality uses that −log⁡(1/V)=log⁡V-\log(1/V)=\log V is a constant and pulls out of the expectation. The result is independent of p⁡(x,y)p(x,y): it does not assume tokens are uniformly distributed in the data, nor any structure on the conditional p⁡(y∣x)p(y\mid x).

Classification analog.

For a KK-way classifier with uniform output q0​(y∣x)=1/Kq_{0}(y\mid x)=1/K, the same argument gives L0=log⁡KL_{0}=\log K. Next-token prediction over a vocabulary of size VV is the special case K=VK=V, with L0=log⁡VL_{0}=\log V. Per-dataset numerical values are listed in Section 3.1.

Relative-L2L_{2} analog.

For dense regression on zz-normalized targets evaluated under relative-L2L_{2} loss (L=‖u^−u‖2/‖u‖2L=\|\hat{u}-u\|_{2}/\|u\|_{2}, the canonical loss for FNO operator learning [33]), the uninformed baseline is u^≡0\hat{u}\equiv 0 (the conditional-mean prediction under no information about the input, which is zero on zz-normalized targets), giving L0=‖0−u‖2/‖u‖2=1L_{0}=\|0-u\|_{2}/\|u\|_{2}=1 exactly. This is the value used for the Darcy experiment (Appendix D.3). The same wrapper h/(1+h)h/(1+h) caps the predicted relative-L2L_{2} at the uninformed baseline as h→∞h\to\infty.

Scale equivariance.

Because L0L_{0} enters the form as a unit-bearing constant rather than a free parameter, the form is equivariant under uniform rescaling of the loss. If L′=k​LL^{\prime}=kL for any constant k>0k>0, then E′=k​EE^{\prime}=kE and L0′=k​L0L_{0}^{\prime}=kL_{0}, and Equation (2) substitutes consistently:

L′=k​L=k⁡[E+(L0−E)​h1+h]=E′+(L0′−E′)​h1+h.L^{\prime}\;=\;kL\;=\;k\!\left[E+(L_{0}-E)\,\frac{h}{1+h}\right]\;=\;E^{\prime}+(L_{0}^{\prime}-E^{\prime})\,\frac{h}{1+h}.

Because hh is dimensionless, the fitted exponents and coefficients (a,b,c,α,β,γ,δ)(a,b,c,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta) are invariant under L→k​LL\to kL. Switching cross-entropy units from nats to bits (k=1/ln⁡2k=1/\ln 2), or applying any uniform rescaling to the loss, leaves the calibrated form intact. Loss types without a natural uninformed-baseline ceiling (e.g., MSE on unnormalized targets, where the appropriate L0L_{0} depends on Var⁡(y)\mathrm{Var}(y) rather than the loss type alone) need normalization before fitting; the relative-L2L_{2} convention above (L0=1L_{0}=1) is the canonical normalization for dense regression.

A.2 Limit verification

Restated for convenience, Equation (2) is

L⁡(N,D,T)=E+(L0−E)⋅h⁡(N,D,T)1+h⁡(N,D,T),h=aNα+bTβ+c​NγDδ,L(N,D,T)=E+(L_{0}-E)\cdot\frac{h(N,D,T)}{1+h(N,D,T)},\qquad h=\frac{a}{N^{\alpha}}+\frac{b}{T^{\beta}}+c\,\frac{N^{\gamma}}{D^{\delta}},

with all parameters (L0,E,a,b,c,α,β,γ,δ)(L_{0},E,a,b,c,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta) non-negative. The wrapper w⁡(h)=h/(1+h)w(h)=h/(1+h) maps [0,∞)[0,\infty) monotonically to [0,1)[0,1), so LL is automatically bounded in [E,L0][E,L_{0}] for any value of the inputs.

Rows 1–5 (L→L0L\to L_{0}).

The three terms in hh are non-negative, so h→∞h\to\infty whenever any one term diverges, and the wrapper saturates: L→L0L\to L_{0}. Each of the first five rows of Table 1 sends exactly one term to infinity:

  • •

    Row 1 (N→0N\to 0; D,TD,T finite): a/Nα→∞a/N^{\alpha}\to\infty.

  • •

    Row 2 (D→0D\to 0; N,TN,T finite): c​Nγ/Dδ→∞c\,N^{\gamma}/D^{\delta}\to\infty for any N>0N>0.

  • •

    Row 3 (T→0T\to 0; N,DN,D finite): b/Tβ→∞b/T^{\beta}\to\infty.

  • •

    Row 4 (N→∞N\to\infty; D,TD,T finite): c​Nγ/Dδ→∞c\,N^{\gamma}/D^{\delta}\to\infty since DD is finite.

  • •

    Row 5 (N,T→∞N,T\to\infty; DD finite): same as row 4 via the overfitting term, irrespective of TT.

Row 6 (L→EL\to E).

This row asks for h→0h\to 0, which requires all three terms in hh to vanish simultaneously. The capacity term a/Nαa/N^{\alpha} vanishes as N→∞N\to\infty and the undertraining term b/Tβb/T^{\beta} vanishes as T→∞T\to\infty, but the overfitting term c​Nγ/Dδc\,N^{\gamma}/D^{\delta} vanishes only along paths in which DδD^{\delta} outpaces NγN^{\gamma}. The form therefore satisfies row 6 as a path-dependent limit: along any joint path with N,T,D→∞N,T,D\to\infty such that Nγ/Dδ→0N^{\gamma}/D^{\delta}\to 0, we have h→0h\to 0 and L→EL\to E. Paths that fail the third condition (e.g., D∝ND\propto N with γ>δ\gamma>\delta) instead drive L→L0L\to L_{0} via the overfitting term. Row 6 thus asserts the existence of a valid path, not pass-anywhere behavior, matching the empirical observation that joint scaling approaches the irreducible loss only when data scales fast enough relative to model size.

A.3 Chinchilla recovery

Proposition 1.

Under three conditions, (i) the single-epoch convention T=DT=D, (ii) small hh (h≤0.1h\leq 0.1), and (iii) negligible overfitting (c​Nγ/Dδ≪a/Nαc\,N^{\gamma}/D^{\delta}\ll a/N^{\alpha}), Equation (2) reduces to Equation (1) up to O⁡(h2)O(h^{2}) corrections, with the same exponents (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) and parameter map

A=(L0−E)​a,B=(L0−E)​b.A=(L_{0}-E)\,a,\qquad B=(L_{0}-E)\,b. (6)

Derivation.

The single-epoch convention T=DT=D collapses our TT axis onto Chinchilla’s DD axis: the undertraining term reduces to b/Tβ=b/Dβb/T^{\beta}=b/D^{\beta}, and the full hh becomes

h=aNα+bDβ+c​NγDδ.h=\frac{a}{N^{\alpha}}+\frac{b}{D^{\beta}}+c\,\frac{N^{\gamma}}{D^{\delta}}.

At Chinchilla-optimal allocations N/D≈1/20N/D\approx 1/20. For the overfitting term to be negligible compared to the capacity term, we require

c​NγDδ≪aNα,i.e.,c≪a⋅DδNα+γ.c\,\frac{N^{\gamma}}{D^{\delta}}\ll\frac{a}{N^{\alpha}},\quad\text{i.e.,}\quad c\ll\frac{a\cdot D^{\delta}}{N^{\alpha+\gamma}}.

With Chinchilla-scale N≈1010N\approx 10^{10}, D≈2×1011D\approx 2\times 10^{11}, α≈0.34\alpha\approx 0.34, and illustrative (γ,δ)=(0.5,1.0)(\gamma,\delta)=(0.5,1.0), the bound evaluates to c≪800​ac\ll 800\,a.

Assuming negligibility and h≪1h\ll 1, Taylor expansion of h/(1+h)=h−h2+h3−⋯h/(1+h)=h-h^{2}+h^{3}-\cdots gives, to leading order,

L≈E+(L0−E)​[aNα+bDβ]=E+(L0−E)​aNα+(L0−E)​bDβ.L\approx E+(L_{0}-E)\Bigl[\frac{a}{N^{\alpha}}+\frac{b}{D^{\beta}}\Bigr]=E+\frac{(L_{0}-E)a}{N^{\alpha}}+\frac{(L_{0}-E)b}{D^{\beta}}.

Comparing to Equation (1) gives the parameter map of Equation (6): A=(L0−E)​aA=(L_{0}-E)a and B=(L0−E)​bB=(L_{0}-E)b. Because TT enters Equation (2) directly (not via C/(k​N)C/(kN)), the recovery introduces no architecture-dependent kk factor. The next-order correction is −h2⋅(L0−E)-h^{2}\cdot(L_{0}-E), which at h∼0.05h\sim 0.05 (our illustrative Chinchilla-scale value) is ∼0.02\sim 0.02 nats, smaller than Chinchilla’s reported fitting residuals [24, 41].

A.4 Choice of saturating wrapper

The wrapper h/(1+h)h/(1+h) in Equation (2) is one of several monotone bijections from [0,∞)[0,\infty) to [0,1)[0,1) that satisfy the design constraints in Section 2. The most natural alternative is w⁡(h)=1−e−hw(h)=1-e^{-h}, which shares the endpoints w⁡(0)=0w(0)=0 and w⁡(∞)=1w(\infty)=1, matches the small-hh slope w′​(0)=1w^{\prime}(0)=1 that recovers Chinchilla without rescaling, and introduces no new parameters. Other monotone bijections such as tanh⁡(h)\tanh(h) or sigmoidal forms either need a free slope or saturation-rate parameter; we exclude them on parsimony grounds.

The two differ in their approach to saturation. h/(1+h)h/(1+h) approaches 1 as 1−1/h+O⁡(1/h2)1-1/h+O(1/h^{2}), while 1−e−h1-e^{-h} approaches 1 exponentially. At small hh, both expand as h−κ​h2+O⁡(h3)h-\kappa h^{2}+O(h^{3}) with κ=1\kappa=1 for h/(1+h)h/(1+h) and κ=1/2\kappa=1/2 for 1−e−h1-e^{-h}, so the two have essentially the same Chinchilla-scale behavior; the difference becomes visible only in the over-trained or overfit corner where h≳1h\gtrsim 1.

We default to h/(1+h)h/(1+h) for closed-form simplicity. Its inverse is rational: writing Lrel=(L−E)/(L0−E)L_{\text{rel}}=(L-E)/(L_{0}-E), the inverse wrapper is w−1​(Lrel)=Lrel/(1−Lrel)w^{-1}(L_{\text{rel}})=L_{\text{rel}}/(1-L_{\text{rel}}), used in Equation (15) of Appendix F.2 to map a target loss to the difficulty h∗h^{*} that achieves it during cost-allocation analysis. The analogous inverse for 1−e−h1-e^{-h} is the transcendental −ln⁡(1−Lrel)-\ln(1-L_{\text{rel}}). The Chinchilla-recovery expansion of Proposition 1 likewise has the clean second-order correction −h2-h^{2}, straightforward to bound. Empirically, the two wrappers perform comparably in our evaluations.

A.5 Remarks on capacity and overfitting

Population versus sample.

The undercapacity and overfitting terms in hh are not mutually exclusive. They separate two levels of the hypothesis-data hierarchy: a/Nαa/N^{\alpha} measures how well a hypothesis class of size NN can represent the true population distribution (a property independent of any particular sample), while c​Nγ/Dδc\,N^{\gamma}/D^{\delta} measures the variance of the empirical-risk minimizer around the population minimizer when only DD samples are available, scaled by the model’s capacity to express deviations. A small model on small data can suffer both undercapacity (too little capacity to represent the population) and overfitting (still enough capacity to memorize the sparse samples, since memorizing DD specific points is an easier hypothesis class than approximating the underlying distribution). In the large-N/DN/D limit the overfitting term grows toward memorization in the strict sense: the model fits the training set exactly while failing to generalize.

Overfitting at a single epoch.

At T=DT=D, each example has been seen only once, and in classical statistics, overfitting requires repeated exposure. In modern deep learning, sufficiently large models memorize even single-epoch training data [11, 46], and the memorization rate scales with model capacity. A plausible mechanism: at large NN, a single gradient step has enough degrees of freedom to encode an example into a subset of weights without perturbing the rest of the model, so excess capacity may flow into example-specific encoding rather than population-level features, with validation loss reflecting the resulting gap. On this reading, the c​Nγ/Dδc\,N^{\gamma}/D^{\delta} term tracks the capacity allocated to training-set-specific encoding. The term itself does not depend on TT, but its contribution to the predicted loss varies smoothly with TT via the saturating wrapper: at small TT, it is masked by the dominant undertraining term b/Tβb/T^{\beta}, and at large TT (where undertraining decays), it becomes the floor that the loss approaches. The transition is gradual and not sharp at T=DT=D.

This same mechanism manifests differently across the training trajectory: Tirumala et al. [46] observe verbatim memorization during the first epoch (well before convergence), while Hernandez et al. [21] and Muennighoff et al. [37] document classical train-val divergence at T>DT>D. Both observations are consistent with a single capacity-allocation effect, observed under different criteria. Sub-epoch sample-size effects (T<DT<D) are dominated by the undertraining term b/Tβb/T^{\beta}, since the relevant cost in that regime is the loss decay with each fresh example seen.

Appendix B Baseline forms

We detail the prior parametric scaling laws surveyed in Section 5. For each form, we list its equation (or structural commitment), the motivation, and the free parameters.

Kaplan Eq. 1.5 [26].

L⁡(N,D)=[(Nc/N)αN/αD+Dc/D]αDL(N,D)=[(N_{c}/N)^{\alpha_{N}/\alpha_{D}}+D_{c}/D]^{\alpha_{D}}. The first joint L⁡(N,D)L(N,D) form, derived by combining a power-law fit on each axis. The composite-power structure implies an overfitting ratio of N0.74/DN^{0.74}/D structurally close to our Nγ/DδN^{\gamma}/D^{\delta} term, but bundled inside a non-separable power, so the NN- and DD-axis exponents cannot be fit independently. No explicit L0L_{0} ceiling; L→∞L\to\infty as D→0D\to 0 or N→0N\to 0. 4 free parameters: Nc,Dc,αN,αDN_{c},D_{c},\alpha_{N},\alpha_{D}.

Chinchilla [24].

L⁡(N,D)=E+A/Nα+B/DβL(N,D)=E+A/N^{\alpha}+B/D^{\beta} (Equation (1)). Replaces Kaplan’s composite power with a strictly additive decomposition and an explicit irreducible-loss floor EE. The canonical compute-optimal reference form, calibrated in the data-rich single-epoch regime; we recover it as the small-hh limit of our form (Appendix A.3). 5 free parameters: E,A,B,α,βE,A,B,\alpha,\beta.

Muennighoff [37].

L=E+A/(N′)α+B/(D′)βL=E+A/(N^{\prime})^{\alpha}+B/(D^{\prime})^{\beta} where N′N^{\prime} and D′D^{\prime} are exponentially-saturating effective quantities with fitted saturation scales RD∗R_{D}^{*} and RN∗R_{N}^{*}. The two saturate in different excesses: as repetitions T/DT/D grow, D′→D⋅(1+RD∗)D^{\prime}\to D\cdot(1+R_{D}^{*}); as parameters exceed UNU_{N}, the size compute-optimal for DD unique tokens, N′→UN⋅(1+RN∗)N^{\prime}\to U_{N}\cdot(1+R_{N}^{*}). Extends Chinchilla to multi-epoch training by treating each repetition as adding diminishing effective data rather than a fresh example. Multi-epoch behavior in the data axis only; no overfitting term and no independent TT axis. 7 free parameters: E,A,B,α,β,RD∗,RN∗E,A,B,\alpha,\beta,R_{D}^{*},R_{N}^{*}.

M4 [1].

L=E+(L0−E)/(1+(x/xc)c)L=E+(L_{0}-E)/(1+(x/x_{c})^{c}), a single-axis form bounding L∈[E,L0]L\in[E,L_{0}], where xcx_{c} sets the scale at which the curve turns over and cc its curvature in an input scalar x∈{N,D,C}x\in\{N,D,C\}. The closest structural analog of our wrapper, but single-axis (one scalar xx rather than a joint h⁡(N,D,T)h(N,D,T)), so it cannot decompose loss into separate NN, DD, TT contributions. Our implementation fits 3 free parameters: EE and the two coefficients xc,cM4x_{c},c_{\text{M4}}.

BNSL [10].

A smoothly-broken power law in a composite scalar x⁡(N,D,C)x(N,D,C) with kk empirical breakpoints; each breakpoint adds three free parameters (location, slope change, smoothness). The only baseline able to fit non-monotone L⁡(N)L(N), but the breakpoint locations and shapes are fit, not predicted from (N,D)(N,D) structure; bounds LL in [E,L0][E,L_{0}] only approximately. We evaluate k=1k=1 and k=2k=2 in our refits. 3+3​k3+3k free parameters: 3 base (a,b,c0a,b,c_{0}) + 3 per breakpoint.

Farseer [31].

L⁡(N,T)=exp⁡(a1​Na2+a3)+exp⁡(b1​Nb2+b3)⋅T−exp⁡(c1​Nc2+c3)L(N,T)=\exp(a_{1}N^{a_{2}}+a_{3})+\exp(b_{1}N^{b_{2}}+b_{3})\cdot T^{-\exp(c_{1}N^{c_{2}}+c_{3})} (Eq. 15 of the Farseer paper; their DD axis is total tokens trained on, which corresponds to our TT under their compute-relation convention C≈6​N​TC\approx 6NT). The three exponentials parameterize an NN-dependent irreducible-loss floor, an NN-dependent coefficient on the data term, and an NN-dependent data-axis exponent. Reports state-of-the-art far-compute extrapolation. Single-epoch (T=DT=D). 9 free parameters (all signed): a1,a2,a3,b1,b2,b3,c1,c2,c3a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},b_{1},b_{2},b_{3},c_{1},c_{2},c_{3}.

Appendix C Fitting methodology

C.1 Optimization procedure

Loss function.

For each form, we minimize Huber loss on log-residuals r=log⁡L^−log⁡Lr=\log\hat{L}-\log L with transition at τ=0.05\tau=0.05 nats: ℓ⁡(r)=12​r2\ell(r)=\tfrac{1}{2}r^{2} for |r|≤τ|r|\leq\tau and ℓ⁡(r)=τ⁡(|r|−τ/2)\ell(r)=\tau(|r|-\tau/2) otherwise. Huber is robust against the heavy-tailed residuals near saturation cells where small absolute errors translate to large fractional errors in log space, and degenerates to ordinary least-squares in the small-residual limit. On our form, the fit recovers the eight free parameters (E,a,b,c,α,β,γ,δ)(E,a,b,c,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta); L0L_{0} is fixed by the loss type and not optimized.

Reparameterization.

Rather than fitting our form directly, we apply two reparameterizations to numerically stabilize the optimization.

First, since NN, DD, and TT are typically large numbers, distributed across many orders of magnitude, their exponentiation tightly couples their coefficient to their exponent. Before fitting, we apply a change of coordinates that “centers” each variable by dividing it by the variable’s geometric mean within the training set. This change of variables leaves the functional form, the exponents, and EE untouched, and rescales the three coefficients (a,b,c)(a,b,c) such that:

a′=a/N0α,b′=b/T0β,c′=c​N0γ/D0δ,a^{\prime}=a\,/\,N_{0}^{\alpha},\qquad b^{\prime}=b\,/\,T_{0}^{\beta},\qquad c^{\prime}=c\,N_{0}^{\gamma}\,/\,D_{0}^{\delta}, (7)

where (N0,T0,D0)(N_{0},T_{0},D_{0}) are the geometric means of NN, TT, and DD within the training set.

Second, since h/(1+h)h/(1+h) is the logistic function of log⁡h\log h, we never form hh itself: we accumulate log⁡h\log h from its three log-terms by a log-sum-exp (following Hoffmann et al. [24]), shifted by the largest of them so that no exponential is taken of a positive number, and apply the wrapper to that.

Optimizer and restarts.

The Huber objective is minimized with BFGS on a JAX-jitted gradient in a log-reparameterized parameter space (positive parameters in log; EE through softplus to enforce E≥0E\geq 0). Each point-estimate fit uses 30 random restarts to mitigate local optima (raised to 200 for Farseer, since its non-convex coupled-exponent landscape is more prone to local minima), and reports the best-of-restarts solution. For most forms (Chinchilla, Muennighoff, BNSL, M4, and ours), each restart independently samples a starting point from a per-parameter distribution: E∼𝒰⁡(0.5,3.0)E\sim\mathcal{U}(0.5,3.0), power-law exponents ∼𝒰⁡(0.1,0.7)\sim\mathcal{U}(0.1,0.7), multiplicative coefficients log-uniform on [0.01,1000][0.01,1000] (with break-scale parameters log-uniform on [10,106][10,10^{6}] for BNSL). These heuristic ranges are chosen to cover the published point estimates of each form with generous margin. For Farseer, we sample coefficient ranges wide enough to cover the magnitudes its exponent-nested coefficients take (±100\pm 100 on the coefficient inside the data-term exponential). Restarts that fail to converge are discarded.

Bootstrap protocol.

When deriving confidence intervals, we bootstrap by resampling the training set with replacement 200 times, and refit the form on each resample independently from scratch. We report the lower and upper bounds of the 95% confidence interval using the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of the bootstrap resamples. To bootstrap efficiently, we use 8 restarts per resample for all forms, and 50 for Farseer (instead of 30 and 200 for the point estimate).

C.2 Fitted parameters

Applying the above reparameterization and bootstrap protocol for our form produces the fitted parameters reported in Table 5.

C.3 Parameter identification

Each of the parameters in our form is identified by a different empirical regime, as summarized in Table 6.

Regime decomposition.

Each of the three terms in our form has a regime where the other two are suppressed, so a value sweep of the dominant term isolates the parameter of interest.

The capacity term a/Nαa/N^{\alpha} is the only term that does not vanish as D,T→∞D,T\to\infty, so the Chinchilla envelope (large D,TD,T) isolates a,αa,\alpha by sweeping NN.

The undertraining term b/Tβb/T^{\beta} is the only term that depends on TT at all, so the well-resourced corner (large NN, which kills the capacity term, and D≫Nγ/δD\gg N^{\gamma/\delta}, which kills the overfitting term) isolates b,βb,\beta by sweeping TT.

The overfitting term c​Nγ/Dδc\,N^{\gamma}/D^{\delta} is the only term that grows as DD shrinks, so the data-constrained corner (large TT, which kills the undertraining term, and large NN, which kills the capacity term and boosts the overfitting term) pushes it into dominance at small DD. Isolating it takes two sweeps rather than one: sweeping DD at fixed NN pins δ\delta, and sweeping NN at fixed DD pins γ\gamma. Either sweep alone leaves cc entangled with the exponent it did not vary, fixing only the prefactor c​Nγc\,N^{\gamma} or c/Dδc/D^{\delta}.

Practically, the irreducible loss floor EE is the most challenging parameter to identify, since it requires that NN, DD, and TT are all large simultaneously (the most expensive regime to sample).

The wrapper is strictly monotonic, so hh can be recovered from an observed loss as h=(L−E)/(L0−L)h=(L-E)/(L_{0}-L). That recovery is noise-sensitive at both ends: near the ceiling L0L_{0} and near the floor EE, a wide range of hh produces losses differing by less than measurement noise. Cells at either extreme therefore constrain hh weakly however densely they are sampled, which bootstrap CIs diagnose as wide marginal intervals.

Chinchilla-grid sub-regime.

For a fit restricted to a Chinchilla-style grid (T≈DT\approx D), the recovery map of Equation (6) identifies a,b,α,βa,b,\alpha,\beta within that fit, while c,γ,δc,\gamma,\delta are resolved only weakly: at T=DT=D, the three terms of hh occupy two axes rather than three, so the overfitting term trades against the other two instead of being pinned on its own. When fitting our form to the Chinchilla dataset, the overfitting term survives as a second power law on the data axis with an exponent of its own; it supplies 64%64\% of hh at the grid’s geometric center, at δ=0.182\delta=0.182 against β=1.295\beta=1.295.

Identifying c,γ,δc,\gamma,\delta individually requires a grid that additionally exercises the overfitting regime: small-DD runs at varied NN, multi-epoch runs at varied T/DT/D, or both. When the fitted grid lacks these regimes, the marginal CI on (c,γ,δ)(c,\gamma,\delta) is wide.

Appendix D Our training experiments

This appendix documents the four experimental domains we ran ourselves: MNIST, CIFAR-100, Darcy, and TinyStories.

Conventions shared across domains.

For each run, we measure total training FLOPs CC directly with a FLOPs counter; the form takes TT rather than CC and does not depend on the linear approximation C≈k​N​TC\approx kNT. The four domains differ in how loss measurements are collected. MNIST uses constant LR throughout with no cooldown, so every logged checkpoint is a valid end-state observation: at each checkpoint we record (N,D,Tcheckpoint,Lval∗)(N,D,T_{\text{checkpoint}},L_{\text{val}}^{*}) with Lval∗L_{\text{val}}^{*} the running minimum validation loss, giving one trajectory of points per (N,D)(N,D) cell. CIFAR-100, Darcy, and TinyStories use a Warmup-Stable-Decay schedule [15]: each (N,D)(N,D) cell consists of one constant-LR stable run that feeds multiple cooldown forks at log-spaced TtotalT_{\text{total}} targets, and we record (N,D,Ttotal,Lfinal)(N,D,T_{\text{total}},L_{\text{final}}) once per cooldown. Hägele et al. [15] show that constant LR plus a short late cooldown matches cosine performance and lets a single stable run feed multiple cooldown forks at different total-compute budgets. Stable-phase intermediate checkpoints from these three domains are not used as data points, because the cooldown’s downstream effect makes the intermediate Lval∗L_{\text{val}}^{*} inequivalent to a final-loss observation at the same TT; MNIST’s no-cooldown protocol makes intermediate-checkpoint and end-of-training observations equivalent by construction (so unlike in other grids, all our MNIST trajectory points are valid). We run a single seed per (N,D)(N,D) stable run for CIFAR-100, Darcy, and TinyStories, and 10 seeds per cell for MNIST (per-cell losses averaged before fitting), following standard practice in the scaling-law literature [26, 24, 37, 15]; the bootstrap procedure in Appendix C.1 resamples (N,D,T,L)(N,D,T;L) training-set points to produce confidence intervals on the fitted parameters.

Effective unique-data exposure.

For trace points or cooldown forks where T<DbudgetT<D_{\text{budget}}, the model has only been exposed to at most TT unique training points regardless of how many were prepared in the corpus. We cap D=min⁡(Dbudget,T)D=\min(D_{\text{budget}},T) before fitting so that the form’s overfitting term c​Nγ/Dδc\,N^{\gamma}/D^{\delta} is fed the actually-seen sample count, not the budgeted one; without this cap, the form would treat sub-1-epoch rows as if the model had full access to the prepared corpus, mis-attributing the high observed loss to undertraining alone instead of also to limited data exposure. The cap is engaged on ∼\sim6% of MNIST trace rows (earliest checkpoints on large-DD cells, where TcheckpointT_{\text{checkpoint}} has not yet reached DbudgetD_{\text{budget}}) and ∼\sim17% of TinyStories cooldown forks (smallest-TtotalT_{\text{total}} forks on large-DD cells); CIFAR-100 and Darcy have no sub-1-epoch rows by construction, so the cap has no effect there.
