Validation loss measured on the standard 10,000-image test set.

Training recipe.

SGD with momentum 0.9, weight decay 5×10−45\times 10^{-4}, batch size 128. Peak LR scales with width as 0.1⋅(32/w)1/20.1\cdot(32/w)^{1/2} (anchor-tuned at w=32w=32), held constant after W=200W=200 linear-warmup steps. SGD+momentum is the canonical CIFAR ResNet optimizer [17]; we use constant LR for the stable phase rather than the conventional cosine decay so that the same stable run can feed multiple cooldown forks. We run 5 cooldown forks per stable run, log-spaced over [Tmax/10,Tmax][T_{\text{max}}/10,T_{\text{max}}], with square-root decay over the final 20% of fork compute. We apply standard CIFAR augmentation (random crop 32×3232\times 32 with 4-pixel padding, random horizontal flip).

D.3 Darcy

Description.

PDEBench 2D Darcy flow at β=1.0\beta=1.0 [45], the canonical operator-learning benchmark for parametric elliptic PDEs. The task is to map a scalar permeability field a⁡(x,y)a(x,y) on a 128×128128\times 128 grid to the steady-state pressure field u⁡(x,y)u(x,y) that satisfies −∇⋅(a(x,y)∇u(x,y))=f(x,y)-\nabla\cdot(a(x,y)\nabla u(x,y))=f(x,y) with prescribed boundary conditions. Loss is the relative-L2L_{2} residual (L=‖u^−u‖2/‖u‖2L=\|\hat{u}-u\|_{2}/\|u\|_{2}, the canonical Li 2021 LpLoss (p=2)(p=2)), which gives L0=1L_{0}=1 exactly under zero predictions on zz-normalized targets.

Architecture and grid.

Fourier neural operator (FNO; 33) with fixed depth (nlayer=4n_{\text{layer}}=4) and Fourier modes (nmodes=12n_{\text{modes}}=12), sweeping the hidden channel width w∈{16,24,32,48,64,96}w\in\{16,24,32,48,64,96\} for 6 model configurations spanning ∼90\sim\!90K to ∼3.2\sim\!3.2M params. Unique-data sweep D∈{10,30,100,320,1000,3160,9000}D\in\{10,30,100,320,1000,3160,9000\} (a,u)(a,u) pairs. Total-exposure sweep T∈[3.0×103, 2.0×106]T\in[3.0\times 10^{3},\,2.0\times 10^{6}] pairs seen, with TmaxT_{\text{max}} scaling with DD (5×1045{\times}10^{4} at D=30D=30, 2×1052{\times}10^{5} at D=100D=100, 5×1055{\times}10^{5} at D=320D=320, 10610^{6} at D∈{1000,3160}D\in\{1000,3160\}, 2×1062{\times}10^{6} at D=9000D=9000), spanning T/DT/D from 2.2 epochs to ∼\sim2,000 at the largest fork. Validation loss measured on a fixed 1,000-pair holdout.

Training recipe.

AdamW with β=(0.9,0.999)\beta=(0.9,0.999) and weight decay 10−410^{-4} (FNO defaults), peak LR 10−310^{-3} held flat after W=100W=100 linear-warmup steps, batch size 20 (a,u)(a,u) pairs per step (Li 2021 default), and 10 cooldown forks per stable run (square-root decay over the final 20% of fork compute, log-spaced over [max⁡(Tfork,Tmax/100),Tmax][\max(T_{\text{fork}},T_{\text{max}}/100),T_{\text{max}}]).

D.4 TinyStories

Description.

TinyStories [13] next-token language modeling with a 2K BPE tokenizer trained on the TinyStories corpus (not Eldan & Li’s original 10K GPT-Neo vocabulary; L0=ln⁡2000≈7.60L_{0}=\ln 2000\approx 7.60 nats). TinyStories is the natural setting for fitting the multi-epoch behavior of the form: every cell on the grid admits T≫DT\gg D, so the b/Tβb/T^{\beta} undertraining term and the c​Nγ/Dδc\,N^{\gamma}/D^{\delta} overfitting term are jointly identifiable.

Architecture and grid.

GPT-style decoder-only transformer in the spirit of Eldan and Li [13]. 5 model sizes with (dmodel,nlayer,nhead,dff)∈{(64,4,4,256),(128,4,4,512),(192,6,6,768),(320,8,8,1280),(480,10,8,1920)}(d_{\text{model}},n_{\text{layer}},n_{\text{head}},d_{\text{ff}})\in\{(64,4,4,256),\allowbreak(128,4,4,512),\allowbreak(192,6,6,768),\allowbreak(320,8,8,1280),\allowbreak(480,10,8,1920)\}, giving N∈{344​K,1.1​M,3.1​M,10.6​M,28.8​M}N\in\{344\text{K},\allowbreak 1.1\text{M},\allowbreak 3.1\text{M},\allowbreak 10.6\text{M},\allowbreak 28.8\text{M}\} params. Context length 256 tokens, fixed across runs. Unique-data sweep D∈{104,105,106,107,108,5×108}D\in\{10^{4},10^{5},10^{6},10^{7},10^{8},5{\times}10^{8}\} unique tokens, giving 30 stable (N,D)(N,D) runs and 300 cooldown-fork final-loss measurements. Total-exposure sweep T∈[2.0×106, 2.5×109]T\in[2.0\times 10^{6},\,2.5\times 10^{9}] tokens seen, with TmaxT_{\text{max}} scaling per cell from 5×1075\times 10^{7} tokens at the smallest DD to 2.5×1092.5\times 10^{9} at the largest, spanning T/DT/D up to ∼\sim5,000 epochs at the largest fork. 17%17\% of rows are sub-epoch in the prepared corpus, reaching T/Dbudget=0.05T/D_{\text{budget}}=0.05 at the smallest forks of the large-DD cells. Those rows enter the fit at D=TD=T under the cap above. Validation loss measured on a fixed 2,000-document holdout from the TinyStories validation split.

Training recipe.

AdamW with β=(0.9,0.95)\beta=(0.9,0.95) and weight decay 0.10.1 (GPT-style defaults), peak LR 3×10−43\times 10^{-4} held flat after W=500W=500 linear-warmup steps, batch size 64 sequences of 256-token context =16,384=16{,}384 tokens per step (fixed across configs), and 10 cooldown forks per stable run (square-root decay over the final 20% of fork compute, log-spaced over [max⁡(Tfork,Tmax/100),Tmax][\max(T_{\text{fork}},T_{\text{max}}/100),T_{\text{max}}]). Note: a config drift on the later 30M-size submission set W=100W=100 for those runs instead of 500; recorded loss is the post-cooldown final-loss, dominated by the late-training trajectory rather than the warmup duration, so LL at any shared TtotalT_{\text{total}} is unaffected.

Appendix E External refits

This appendix documents the five published LLM scaling-law grids we refit our form to: Chinchilla, Muennighoff, Gadre, Porian, and Farseer. In each case, the grid covers only a subset of the (N,D,T)(N,D,T) space that our form parameterizes.

E.1 Chinchilla

Description.

Hoffmann et al. [24], transcribed by Besiroglu et al. [7] from DeepMind’s published Approach-3 isoFLOP figures (raw isoFLOP sweep was never released). The canonical compute-optimal reference grid for the Chinchilla parametric form. Single-epoch training (T=DT=D throughout).

Architecture and grid.

Decoder-only transformers; tokenizer is a 32K SentencePiece vocabulary on MassiveText (L0=10.373L_{0}=10.373). 245 rows spanning N∈[5.73×107,1.62×1010]N\in[5.73\times 10^{7},1.62\times 10^{10}] params and D∈[2.45×108,3.18×1011]D\in[2.45\times 10^{8},3.18\times 10^{11}] tokens at Chinchilla-optimal and near-optimal compute.

Training recipe.

As reported by Hoffmann et al. [24]: cosine LR schedule with warmup, AdamW, single epoch over MassiveText. Loss is cross-entropy nats per token.

E.2 Muennighoff

Description.

Muennighoff et al. [37], source data is the NAMES_TO_VAL_LOSSES dict in HuggingFace’s datablations repository (lm1-misc/parametric_fit.ipynb). The only public grid with T>DT>D (multi-epoch repetition).

Architecture and grid.

Decoder-only transformers on C4; 50,257-token GPT-NeoX/GPT-2 vocabulary (L0=10.825L_{0}=10.825). The source data holds 324 rows; averaging the replicate runs that share an (N,D,T)(N,D,T) cell leaves 232 rows, spanning N∈[7.10×106,8.67×109]N\in[7.10\times 10^{6},8.67\times 10^{9}] params and D∈[1.00×108,1.78×1011]D\in[1.00\times 10^{8},1.78\times 10^{11}] tokens. Most cells are single runs (214 of the 232) and the 18 replicated cells carry 2 to 17 rows each. Replicates agree closely in most of those cells (median spread 0.0270.027 nats), but not in all: three spread by 0.170.17 to 0.360.36 nats, which is the same size as the held-out RMSE any form attains on this grid, so the averages in those three cells should not be read as precise measurements. The grid runs T/D>1T/D>1 in 198 of its 232 rows, at 23 distinct values of DD from 1.00×1081.00\times 10^{8} to 8.80×10108.80\times 10^{10}, reaching T/D=9000T/D=9000 at the most repeated cells.

Training recipe.

As reported by Muennighoff et al. [37]: cosine LR schedule, AdamW, multi-epoch passes over data-constrained subsets of C4. Loss is cross-entropy nats per token.

E.3 Gadre

Description.

Gadre et al. [14], published CSV at mlfoundations/scaling. The over-trained-regime grid: single-epoch models sweeping the token multiplier M=D/NM=D/N from ∼5\sim\!5, below Chinchilla-optimal, up to ∼640\sim\!640. The published CSV mixes three corpora at the same (N,D)(N,D); we filter to rw_original (RefinedWeb) to match Porian’s corpus and enable direct over-trained-vs-Kaplan comparison. Single epoch (T=DT=D).

Architecture and grid.

Decoder-only transformers on RefinedWeb; 50,432-token vocabulary (L0=10.828L_{0}=10.828; recoverable from their released params and params_no_embed fields, whose difference divided by the model width is exactly 50,432 at every width). The published CSV holds 104 rows across three corpora (35 rw_original, 35 rpj, 34 c4_original); the corpus filter leaves only 35 rows, spanning N∈[1.06×107,6.89×109]N\in[1.06\times 10^{7},6.89\times 10^{9}] params and D∈[5.28×107,4.61×1011]D\in[5.28\times 10^{7},4.61\times 10^{11}] tokens. This is the smallest of our nine grids by a wide margin, and the high-CC and high-DD protocols hold out 4 cells each, so its held-out RMSE carries correspondingly more sampling noise than the other columns, and we do not read a narrow margin on this grid as meaningful.

Training recipe.

As reported by Gadre et al. [14]: cosine LR schedule with linear warmup, AdamW, single-epoch over RefinedWeb. Loss is cross-entropy nats per token.

E.4 Porian

Description.

Porian et al. [41], used as a Kaplan stand-in (Kaplan’s 2020 raw data is not public). Porian re-runs Chinchilla-style training under several LR schedules including a Kaplan-style decay-to-fixed-TmaxT_{\text{max}}.

Architecture and grid.

Decoder-only transformers on RefinedWeb; 32K SentencePiece tokenizer (L0=10.373L_{0}=10.373). 238 rows after filtering to the rw|base|long_warmup|kaplan_decay subset (the closest reproduction of Kaplan-style training; other protocols dropped to avoid mixing schedules in one fit), spanning N∈[3.32×105,9.02×108]N\in[3.32\times 10^{5},9.02\times 10^{8}] params and D∈[5.05×106,2.86×1010]D\in[5.05\times 10^{6},2.86\times 10^{10}] tokens, with a denser experimental grid near the compute-optimal frontier. Single epoch (T=DT=D).

Training recipe.

As reported by Porian et al. [41]: long-warmup cosine schedule with optional Kaplan-style decay-to-fixed-TmaxT_{\text{max}}, AdamW with carefully tuned batch size and LR, single epoch over RefinedWeb. Loss is cross-entropy nats per token.

E.5 Farseer

Description.

Li et al. [31]: the largest single-recipe scaling-law dataset publicly available (404 dense-LM runs, single-epoch, cosine-to-zero LR schedule). We use the authors’ 1222_full.csv release, scored on their held-out IntelliValSet_Raw bits-per-character measure. Four (N,D,T)(N,D,T) cells hold two rows each, and we average them, resulting in a 400-cell cohort.

Architecture and grid.

Dense decoder-only transformers; 65,536-token tokenizer on a web + math + code mixture. We fit the bits-per-character loss their paper reports rather than cross-entropy nats, which sets the saturating ceiling at L0=log2⁡(65,536)/4=4.0L_{0}=\log_{2}(65{,}536)/4=4.0 bits/char, assuming a mixture averaging 4 characters per token. 400 cells, spanning N∈[9.96×107,6.37×109]N\in[9.96\times 10^{7},6.37\times 10^{9}] params and D∈[1.00×109,5.12×1011]D\in[1.00\times 10^{9},5.12\times 10^{11}] tokens. Single-epoch (T=DT=D).

Training recipe.

As reported by Li et al. [31]: cosine-to-zero LR schedule with warmup, AdamW, single-epoch over the web/math/code mixture. Loss is bits per character.

Appendix F Cost-aware allocation

F.1 Compute-optimal model size at fixed unique data

We derive the optimal model size N∗N^{*} at fixed unique data DD under our form, in two regimes: the asymptotic limit T→∞T\to\infty, and the finite-compute case using the planning approximation C≈k​N​TC\approx kNT. We then verify that no other parametric scaling law referenced in this paper admits an analogous interior minimum in NN at fixed DD.

Asymptotic optimum (T→∞T\to\infty).

At fixed DD as T→∞T\to\infty, the undertraining term b/Tβb/T^{\beta} vanishes and

h∞​(N,D)=aNα+c​NγDδ.h_{\infty}(N,D)=\frac{a}{N^{\alpha}}+\frac{c\,N^{\gamma}}{D^{\delta}}.

The stationarity condition ∂h∞/∂N=0\partial h_{\infty}/\partial N=0 gives

−α​aNα+1+γ​c​Nγ−1Dδ=0⟹N∞∗​(D)=(α​a​Dδγ​c)1/(α+γ).-\frac{\alpha a}{N^{\alpha+1}}+\frac{\gamma c\,N^{\gamma-1}}{D^{\delta}}=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad N^{*}_{\infty}(D)=\left(\frac{\alpha a\,D^{\delta}}{\gamma c}\right)^{1/(\alpha+\gamma)}. (8)

This is an interior minimum:

∂2h∞∂N2=α⁡(α+1)​aNα+2+γ⁡(γ−1)​c​Nγ−2Dδ,\frac{\partial^{2}h_{\infty}}{\partial N^{2}}=\alpha(\alpha+1)\frac{a}{N^{\alpha+2}}+\gamma(\gamma-1)\frac{c\,N^{\gamma-2}}{D^{\delta}},

which is positive at N∞∗N^{*}_{\infty} for α,γ>0\alpha,\gamma>0 and a,c>0a,c>0: substituting the stationarity condition gives ∂2h∞/∂N2=α⁡(α+γ)​a/Nα+2>0\partial^{2}h_{\infty}/\partial N^{2}=\alpha(\alpha+\gamma)\,a/N^{\alpha+2}>0 at N=N∞∗N=N^{*}_{\infty}. Below N∞∗N^{*}_{\infty}, the undercapacity term dominates and increasing NN helps; above N∞∗N^{*}_{\infty}, the overfitting term dominates and increasing NN raises the asymptotic loss. Because the wrapper h/(1+h)h/(1+h) is monotone, the same N∞∗N^{*}_{\infty} minimizes LL itself.

Finite-compute optimum.

Using T=C/(k​N)T=C/(kN), at fixed C,DC,D we minimize

h⁡(N,D,C)=aNα+b​kβ​NβCβ+c​NγDδ.h(N,D,C)=\frac{a}{N^{\alpha}}+\frac{b\,k^{\beta}\,N^{\beta}}{C^{\beta}}+\frac{c\,N^{\gamma}}{D^{\delta}}.

Setting ∂h/∂N=0\partial h/\partial N=0 gives the implicit relation

α​a=β​b​kβ​N∗α+βCβ+γ​c​N∗α+γDδ,\alpha a\;=\;\frac{\beta\,b\,k^{\beta}\,N^{*\,\alpha+\beta}}{C^{\beta}}\;+\;\frac{\gamma c\,N^{*\,\alpha+\gamma}}{D^{\delta}}, (9)

which has a unique solution since the right-hand side is monotone increasing in NN from 00 at N=0N=0 to ∞\infty. Two limits recover the boundary behavior:

Limit D→∞D\to\infty (data-rich, Chinchilla regime). The third term in Equation (9) vanishes, giving

N∗​(C)=(α​a​Cββ​b​kβ)1/(α+β)∝Cβ/(α+β).N^{*}(C)=\left(\frac{\alpha a\,C^{\beta}}{\beta\,b\,k^{\beta}}\right)^{1/(\alpha+\beta)}\;\propto\;C^{\beta/(\alpha+\beta)}. (10)

With Chinchilla-like exponents α≈β\alpha\approx\beta, N∗​(C)∝C1/2N^{*}(C)\propto C^{1/2}, recovering Hoffmann et al. [24]’s compute-optimal scaling.

Limit C→∞C\to\infty at fixed DD. The second term in Equation (9) vanishes, recovering N∞∗​(D)N^{*}_{\infty}(D) from Equation (8). The compute-optimal model size therefore saturates at a finite value as compute grows past the point at which adding capacity costs more in overfitting than it gains in undercapacity reduction. This is the data-constrained shift qualitatively documented by Muennighoff et al. [37]: spending more compute on a fixed unique-data pool eventually requires shrinking the model rather than enlarging it.

Other parametric forms.

Among the parametric scaling laws of Section 5, none admits a non-trivial N∗N^{*} at fixed DD as T→∞T\to\infty:

  • •

    Chinchilla. L=E+A/Nα+B/DβL=E+A/N^{\alpha}+B/D^{\beta} is monotone non-increasing in NN.

  • •

    Kaplan Eq. 1.5. L=[(Nc/N)αN/αD+Dc/D]αDL=[(N_{c}/N)^{\alpha_{N}/\alpha_{D}}+D_{c}/D]^{\alpha_{D}}. As N→∞N\to\infty the first bracket term vanishes and L→(Dc/D)αDL\to(D_{c}/D)^{\alpha_{D}}; monotone non-increasing in NN.

  • •

    Muennighoff. L=E+A/(N′)α+B/(D′)βL=E+A/(N^{\prime})^{\alpha}+B/(D^{\prime})^{\beta} with effective N′N^{\prime} saturating at N⁡(1+RN∗)N(1+R_{N}^{*}) as N→∞N\to\infty. Both terms are monotone non-increasing in NN.

  • •

    M4. Single-axis form, monotone by construction.

  • •

    Farseer. NN-dependent exponents but no overfitting term; inherits Chinchilla’s monotonicity in NN.

  • •

    BNSL. Can express non-monotone behavior via empirical breakpoints, but the breakpoint locations and shapes are fit, not predicted from (N,D)(N,D) structure.

The U-shape in L⁡(N)L(N) at fixed DD is therefore a structural feature unique to our form among the reference set, and matches the empirical observation of Hernandez et al. [21] that validation loss is non-monotone in capacity under heavy data repetition.

F.2 Cost-optimal allocation

A calibrated scaling law lets us answer two reciprocal practitioner questions: (P1) given a target validation loss L∗L^{*}, what is the minimum dollar cost ℬ∗\mathcal{B}^{*} to reach it, and how should that budget split across model size NN, unique data DD, and training duration TT? (P2) given a fixed dollar budget ℬmax\mathcal{B}_{\text{max}}, what is the lowest validation loss achievable, and what allocation achieves it? When training compute is the sole cost (the Chinchilla setup), (P1) and (P2) collapse to dual readouts of the compute-optimal frontier. When unique data must be generated, labeled, or licensed at non-trivial per-example cost, both require joint optimization over (N,D,T)(N,D,T) with two independent cost terms.

Setup.

Let ρD\rho_{D} be the dollar cost per unique training example (label, simulation run, scraped token, etc.) and ρC\rho_{C} the dollar cost per FLOP. Using the standard approximation C≈k​N​TC\approx kNT, the dollar cost is

ℬ⁡(N,D,T)=ρD⋅D+ρC⋅k​N​T.\mathcal{B}(N,D,T)=\rho_{D}\cdot D+\rho_{C}\cdot kNT. (11)

Both (P1) and (P2) are smooth constrained optimizations on ℝ>03\mathbb{R}^{3}_{>0} under our form L=E+(L0−E)​h/(1+h)L=E+(L_{0}-E)\,h/(1+h) with h=a/Nα+b/Tβ+c​Nγ/Dδh=a/N^{\alpha}+b/T^{\beta}+c\,N^{\gamma}/D^{\delta}. They are duals (the same Lagrangian governs both), so the optimal allocation (N∗,D∗,T∗)(N^{*},D^{*},T^{*}) that solves (P1) at target L∗L^{*} also solves (P2) at budget ℬ∗​(L∗)\mathcal{B}^{*}(L^{*}).

(P1) Target-loss optimum.

Form the Lagrangian ℒ1=ℬ+μ⁡(L−L∗)\mathcal{L}_{1}=\mathcal{B}+\mu(L-L^{*}) with μ≥0\mu\geq 0. Setting ∂ℒ1/∂X=0\partial\mathcal{L}_{1}/\partial X=0 for X∈{N,D,T}X\in\{N,D,T\} gives the stationarity conditions

−ρC​k​T∂L/∂N=−ρD∂L/∂D=−ρC​k​N∂L/∂T=μ,-\frac{\rho_{C}kT}{\partial L/\partial N}\;=\;-\frac{\rho_{D}}{\partial L/\partial D}\;=\;-\frac{\rho_{C}kN}{\partial L/\partial T}\;=\;\mu, (12)

i.e., equate the marginal dollar cost per unit of loss reduction across all three axes (the minus signs render μ≥0\mu\geq 0 since ∂L/∂X<0\partial L/\partial X<0 at any interior optimum). Combined with the loss constraint L⁡(N,D,T)=L∗L(N,D,T)=L^{*}, Equation (12) pins down a unique (N∗,D∗,T∗)(N^{*},D^{*},T^{*}). Substituting into Equation (11) gives ℬ∗​(L∗)=ρD​D∗+ρC​k​N∗​T∗\mathcal{B}^{*}(L^{*})=\rho_{D}D^{*}+\rho_{C}kN^{*}T^{*}, the minimum dollar spend to reach L∗L^{*}.

(P2) Budget-constrained optimum.

Form ℒ2=L+λ⁡(ℬ−ℬmax)\mathcal{L}_{2}=L+\lambda(\mathcal{B}-\mathcal{B}_{\text{max}}) with λ≥0\lambda\geq 0. The stationarity conditions are

∂L/∂NρC​k​T=∂L/∂DρD=∂L/∂TρC​k​N=−λ,\frac{\partial L/\partial N}{\rho_{C}kT}\;=\;\frac{\partial L/\partial D}{\rho_{D}}\;=\;\frac{\partial L/\partial T}{\rho_{C}kN}\;=\;-\lambda, (13)

i.e., equate the marginal loss reduction per dollar across all three axes. Together with ℬ⁡(N,D,T)=ℬmax\mathcal{B}(N,D,T)=\mathcal{B}_{\text{max}} this pins down (N∗,D∗,T∗)(N^{*},D^{*},T^{*}) and yields L∗=L⁡(N∗,D∗,T∗)L^{*}=L(N^{*},D^{*},T^{*}). The two sets of stationarity conditions are reciprocals (Equation (12) divides what Equation (13) multiplies), so the two optima trace out the same Pareto frontier {(ℬ∗,L∗)}\{(\mathcal{B}^{*},L^{*})\} and either problem can be read off the other.

Data already in hand.

A practitioner who already holds D0D_{0} examples pays only for what they generate on top of them, so the budget becomes

ℬ⁡(N,D,T)=ρD⋅(D−D0)+ρC⋅k​N​T,D≥D0,\mathcal{B}(N,D,T)=\rho_{D}\cdot(D-D_{0})+\rho_{C}\cdot kNT,\qquad D\geq D_{0}, (14)

and D0=0D_{0}=0 recovers Equation (11). Restricting to D≥D0D\geq D_{0} rules out nothing worth considering: training on fewer examples than one already has refunds no money, since the budget pays only for generation beyond D0D_{0}, and raises the loss, since ∂L/∂D<0\partial L/\partial D<0. Both problems’ stationarity conditions are unchanged, because ∂ℬ/∂D=ρD\partial\mathcal{B}/\partial D=\rho_{D} either way. A sunk cost shifts the objective by a constant, leaving the marginal condition unchanged. So whenever the unconstrained optimum satisfies D∗≥D0D^{*}\geq D_{0}, (P1) returns the same (N∗,D∗,T∗)(N^{*},D^{*},T^{*}) and reports a cost lower by ρD​D0\rho_{D}D_{0}, and (P2) under budget ℬmax\mathcal{B}_{\text{max}} is exactly (P2) with no existing data under budget ℬmax+ρD​D0\mathcal{B}_{\text{max}}+\rho_{D}D_{0}.

Feasibility and boundary behavior.

The form’s [E,L0][E,L_{0}] ceiling makes infeasibility of (P1) detectable in closed form. Inverting the wrapper, the difficulty hh required to hit a target L∗L^{*} is

h∗=L∗−EL0−L∗,h^{*}\;=\;\frac{L^{*}-E}{L_{0}-L^{*}}, (15)

which is positive and finite iff L∗∈(E,L0)L^{*}\in(E,L_{0}). Outside this open interval the constraint manifold {(N,D,T):L⁡(N,D,T)=L∗}\{(N,D,T):L(N,D,T)=L^{*}\} is empty:

  • •

    L∗<EL^{*}<E: asks for a model below the irreducible loss; (P1) has no solution. The Lagrangian’s stationarity conditions become inconsistent and the Newton iteration diverges or stalls. To diagnose this, compute h∗h^{*} and check the sign.

  • •

    L∗≥L0L^{*}\geq L_{0}: trivially achievable by an untrained model. The optimizer pushes one of a/Nαa/N^{\alpha}, b/Tβb/T^{\beta}, or c​Nγ/Dδc\,N^{\gamma}/D^{\delta} toward infinity (e.g., T→0T\to 0), so ℬ∗→0\mathcal{B}^{*}\to 0. (P1) at this target is well-defined but uninformative.

  • •

    L∗→E+L^{*}\to E^{+}: h∗→0h^{*}\to 0, which requires a/Nα+b/Tβ+c​Nγ/Dδ→0a/N^{\alpha}+b/T^{\beta}+c\,N^{\gamma}/D^{\delta}\to 0 jointly. This forces N→∞N\to\infty and T→∞T\to\infty, with D→∞D\to\infty along a path where DδD^{\delta} outpaces NγN^{\gamma} in the overfitting term (see Appendix A.2, Row 6). The cost ℬ∗→∞\mathcal{B}^{*}\to\infty. So L∗=EL^{*}=E is a limit point of the feasible region.

Within the feasible interior L∗∈(E,L0)L^{*}\in(E,L_{0}), the optimum is attained at finite (N∗,D∗,T∗)(N^{*},D^{*},T^{*}). At any fixed DD, the form admits a finite interior minimum N∗​(D)N^{*}(D) from the U-shape competition between the capacity term and the overfitting term (Appendix F.1 derives N∞∗​(D)=(α​a​Dδ/γ​c)1/(α+γ)N^{*}_{\infty}(D)=(\alpha aD^{\delta}/\gamma c)^{1/(\alpha+\gamma)} in the asymptotic T→∞T\to\infty limit), achieving L∗​(D)>EL^{*}(D)>E at that finite N∗​(D)N^{*}(D). The family {L∗​(D):D>0}\{L^{*}(D):D>0\} traces out an achievable frontier that approaches EE only as D→∞D\to\infty. (P1) at any target above this frontier has a finite-allocation solution; only L∗=EL^{*}=E requires the joint ∞\infty limit. The numerical solver should compute h∗h^{*} first via Equation (15) and reject targets outside (E,L0)(E,L_{0}) before iterating.

Recipe.

The general system has no closed form, so we solve numerically. The procedure for either (P1) or (P2):

  1. 1.

    Calibrate the form on a domain-specific training grid to obtain (E,a,b,c,α,β,γ,δ)(E,a,b,c,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta) and L0L_{0} (Section 3).

  2. 2.

    Specify the price pair (ρD,ρC)(\rho_{D},\rho_{C}) for the deployment setting and an architecture-dependent FLOP-per-step constant kk.

  3. 3.

    Solve Equation (12) (for P1) or (13) (for P2) jointly with the active constraint over (N,D,T)(N,D,T) until the stationarity conditions hold to tolerance.

  4. 4.

    Read off the dual quantities: ℬ∗\mathcal{B}^{*} and (N∗,D∗,T∗,T∗/D∗)(N^{*},D^{*},T^{*},T^{*}/D^{*}) for P1, or L∗L^{*} and the same allocation for P2.

Cost ratios and the data-constrained regime.

A useful summary statistic is the dollar-cost ratio η=ρD/ρC\eta=\rho_{D}/\rho_{C}. For LLM pretraining on web-scraped data, η\eta is small (data is cheap, compute dominates) and the Chinchilla-style optimum approximates both (P1) and (P2). For physical-simulation surrogates, RL data generation, and expert label acquisition, η\eta is large (each example is expensive). As η\eta grows, the optimum shifts toward smaller DD (fewer expensive examples), more epochs, and more compute spent revisiting the same data.

Compute is not exactly proportional to dollars.

Equation (11) treats compute as linear in dollars via a constant ρC\rho_{C}, but in practice users pay for GPU-hours, not FLOPs. For instance, small models cannot fully utilize a multi-GPU node, and large models incur communication overhead. The apparent ρC\rho_{C} therefore depends on NN and on the cluster topology. Accurate cost-aware fits should treat ρC​(N)\rho_{C}(N) as a function calibrated to the actual hardware.

Stationarity conditions in terms of ∂h\partial h.

The partial derivatives of h=a/Nα+b/Tβ+c​Nγ/Dδh=a/N^{\alpha}+b/T^{\beta}+c\,N^{\gamma}/D^{\delta} are

∂h∂N=−α​aNα+1+γ​c​Nγ−1Dδ,∂h∂D=−δ​c​NγDδ+1,∂h∂T=−β​bTβ+1,\frac{\partial h}{\partial N}=-\frac{\alpha a}{N^{\alpha+1}}+\frac{\gamma c\,N^{\gamma-1}}{D^{\delta}},\quad\frac{\partial h}{\partial D}=-\frac{\delta c\,N^{\gamma}}{D^{\delta+1}},\quad\frac{\partial h}{\partial T}=-\frac{\beta b}{T^{\beta+1}},

and ∂L/∂X=(L0−E)​(∂h/∂X)/(1+h)2\partial L/\partial X=(L_{0}-E)(\partial h/\partial X)/(1+h)^{2} for X∈{N,D,T}X\in\{N,D,T\}. Substituting into Equations (12) and (13) gives the stationarity conditions in terms of ∂h\partial h:

(P2):\displaystyle\text{(P2)}:\quad 1ρC​k​T​∂h∂N=1ρD​∂h∂D=1ρC​k​N​∂h∂T=−λ​(1+h)2(L0−E),\displaystyle\frac{1}{\rho_{C}kT}\frac{\partial h}{\partial N}=\frac{1}{\rho_{D}}\frac{\partial h}{\partial D}=\frac{1}{\rho_{C}kN}\frac{\partial h}{\partial T}=-\frac{\lambda(1+h)^{2}}{(L_{0}-E)}, (16)
(P1):\displaystyle\text{(P1)}:\quad ρC​k​T⋅(∂h∂N)−1=ρD⋅(∂h∂D)−1=ρC​k​N⋅(∂h∂T)−1=−μ⁡(L0−E)(1+h)2,\displaystyle\rho_{C}kT\cdot\left(\frac{\partial h}{\partial N}\right)^{-1}=\rho_{D}\cdot\left(\frac{\partial h}{\partial D}\right)^{-1}=\rho_{C}kN\cdot\left(\frac{\partial h}{\partial T}\right)^{-1}=-\frac{\mu(L_{0}-E)}{(1+h)^{2}}, (17)

each system four equations in four unknowns ({N∗,D∗,T∗,λ}\{N^{*},D^{*},T^{*},\lambda\} for P2, replacing λ\lambda with μ\mu for P1, with μ=1/λ\mu=1/\lambda at the dual optimum).

Asymptotic regimes.

(i) When ρD≫ρC\rho_{D}\gg\rho_{C} (data dominates cost): D∗D^{*} is small, multi-epoch training is preferred, T∗T^{*} scales freely until the overfitting term c​Nγ/Dδc\,N^{\gamma}/D^{\delta} saturates the wrapper. (ii) When ρD≪ρC\rho_{D}\ll\rho_{C} (compute dominates cost): the stationarity condition for DD pushes D∗→∞D^{*}\to\infty, the overfitting term vanishes, and (N∗,T∗)(N^{*},T^{*}) approach the Chinchilla compute-optimal allocation in (N,D=T)(N,D{=}T) variables; the Chinchilla single-epoch convention T=DT=D is recovered by selecting DD at the smallest value already killing the overfitting term (once c​Nγ/DδcN^{\gamma}/D^{\delta} is negligible, the loss is invariant under further DD increases).

Log-convexity and uniqueness.

Minimizing LL is equivalent to minimizing h⁡(N,D,T)=a/Nα+b/Tβ+c​Nγ/Dδh(N,D,T)=a/N^{\alpha}+b/T^{\beta}+c\,N^{\gamma}/D^{\delta}, since LL is monotone in hh (the wrapper h/(1+h)h/(1+h) is monotone non-decreasing). Substituting u=log⁡Nu=\log N, v=log⁡Dv=\log D, w=log⁡Tw=\log T, h=a​e−α​u+b​e−β​w+c​eγ​u−δ​vh=a\,e^{-\alpha u}+b\,e^{-\beta w}+c\,e^{\gamma u-\delta v}, a sum of exponentials of linear functions of (u,v,w)(u,v,w), which is convex (each eaffinee^{\text{affine}} term is convex; sum of convex is convex). In fact hh is strictly convex in (u,v,w)(u,v,w) when a,b,c,α,β,γ,δ>0a,b,c,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta>0: its Hessian is block-diagonal in {(u,v),w}\{(u,v),w\}, with the (w,w)(w,w) entry b​β2​e−β​w>0b\beta^{2}e^{-\beta w}>0 and the (u,v)(u,v) block having determinant a​c​α2​δ2​e(γ−α)​u−δ​v>0ac\,\alpha^{2}\delta^{2}e^{(\gamma-\alpha)u-\delta v}>0 and positive trace, so both blocks are positive definite. The dollar cost ℬ=ρD​ev+ρC​k​eu+w\mathcal{B}=\rho_{D}e^{v}+\rho_{C}ke^{u+w} is convex in (u,v,w)(u,v,w), so the feasible set {ℬ≤ℬmax}\{\mathcal{B}\leq\mathcal{B}_{\text{max}}\} is convex. Minimizing a strictly convex function on a convex feasible set yields a unique optimum, so (P1) and (P2) each have a unique solution (N∗,D∗,T∗)(N^{*},D^{*},T^{*}), and standard convex-optimization tools converge to it from any feasible starting point. (At the boundary, c=0c=0 or b=0b=0, the strict convexity fails and the optimum on the DD or TT axis becomes degenerate.)

Appendix G Conformal prediction

When using a fitted form to make a new prediction, we would like to quantify our uncertainty in that prediction. A tempting approach would follow the pattern used when reporting confidence intervals throughout the paper; i.e., redraw bootstrap samples from the training set, refit the form on each, and report the spread of predictions across the ensemble. However, this approach would underestimate the uncertainty of the prediction because the bootstrap interval models the spread of the fit itself, not the spread of a new observation around that fit. The interval shrinks as the number of grid points increases, and it does not capture, for instance, a systematic offset caused by a misspecified form or the inherent variation of noisy observations. Instead, the standard approach is to use conformal prediction to build a calibrated interval for the prediction [48, 30].

Calibration procedure.

Conformal prediction assumes exchangeability of the new prediction and the training set, so to build a calibration set for extrapolation, we must choose a calibration set that lies along the axis we are extrapolating. Rather than creating a single held-out subset, we create many nested subsets for robustness according to the following procedure:

  1. 1.

    Sort the training rows along the axis to be extrapolated.

  2. 2.

    Cut the sorted rows at 40%40\%.

  3. 3.

    Fit the form on the rows below the cut.

  4. 4.

    Divide the rows above the cut into slices of 10%10\%.

  5. 5.

    Predict the loss of every row in every slice above the cut.

  6. 6.

    Record the error log⁡L^−log⁡L\log\hat{L}-\log L of each prediction.

  7. 7.

    Move the cut up by 5%5\%. Do steps 3 to 6 again. Stop when the cut passes 85%85\%.

Once we have gathered all the errors, we read off the quantiles that leave α\alpha of them outside. Writing the sorted errors as r1≤⋯≤rnr_{1}\leq\cdots\leq r_{n}, the 1−α1-\alpha prediction interval for a new point whose predicted loss is L^\hat{L} is

[L^​e−q^+,L^​e−q^−],q^+=r(⌈(n+1)​(1−α/2)⌉),q^−=−(−r)(⌈(n+1)​(1−α/2)⌉),\Big[\,\hat{L}\,e^{-\hat{q}_{+}},\;\;\hat{L}\,e^{-\hat{q}_{-}}\,\Big],\qquad\hat{q}_{+}=r_{(\lceil(n+1)(1-\alpha/2)\rceil)},\quad\hat{q}_{-}=-\big(-r\big)_{(\lceil(n+1)(1-\alpha/2)\rceil)}, (18)

where r(k)r_{(k)} is the kk-th smallest error and α=0.1\alpha=0.1 is the target miss rate. We take α/2\alpha/2 from each tail, so this value of α\alpha gives an asymmetric 90% interval. In our case, to obtain the prediction interval for a new (N,D,T)(N,D,T) cell, compute L^\hat{L} from the fitted form, and multiply it by e−q^+e^{-\hat{q}_{+}} and e−q^−e^{-\hat{q}_{-}} for the lower and upper limit, respectively. In Figures 4 and 5 we show the conformal predictions for the Chinchilla and TinyStories grids, respectively, comparing our form to the Muennighoff, Chinchilla, and Farseer forms.

Appendix H Far extrapolation

While our form is designed to make predictions in the data-constrained regime, one might ask how well it performs in a realistic data-rich LLM scaling prediction regime. Li et al. [31] introduce a dataset of 7 large-model runs held back from the 400 they fit, which are beyond the scope of our main-paper extrapolations. These 7 runs sit 1.71.7 to 5.4×5.4\times beyond the cohort in compute and form the basis of the Farseer “far extrapolation” benchmark, which we reproduce here. We find that when asked to predict these far-compute targets, our form performs as well as Farseer’s own form on the grid it was built specifically for (substantially better than Chinchilla’s form). We report the results in Figure 6 and show conformal intervals (as described in Appendix G) in Figure 7.

Appendix I Full results

I.1 Full experiment results and ablations

The three tables below report each form’s RMSE on each dataset under four protocols: in-sample, the full-dataset fit with no holdout (Table 7); 5-fold cross-validation (Table 8); and high-CC and high-DD holdouts (Table 9, both defined in §3.1). Forms above the horizontal rule are external baselines fit to the loss surface; below the rule, our form (Eq. (2)) and four ablations of it. Datasets to the left of the vertical rule are from our experiments (Section 3); to the right are published grids on which we refit each form.

In-sample fit.

Our form (or one of its wrapper-choice and single-exponent siblings) attains the lowest in-sample RMSE on every column of Table 7. We report this metric for completeness because it is the metric that much of the scaling-law literature focuses on, but it is deliberately not the focus of this paper. A form with three additional free parameters mechanically fits its training set better than a baseline, so its strong performance on this metric is not surprising. The practical use of a fitted scaling law comes instead from extrapolation, not interpolation.

Random 5-fold cross validation.

Random 5-fold tests near-interpolation: each held-out cell is bracketed by training cells on every axis. Our form family wins eight of nine columns (Table 8); the only loss is Chinchilla, where the Muennighoff and Farseer forms have a lower median RMSE.

High-CC and high-DD extrapolation ablations.

Here, we perform ablations of our form to investigate the impact of each component of our form on its prediction performance on our main metrics of interest: high-CC and high-DD extrapolation. In our own training grids that exercise the high T/DT/D regime, we observe the largest degradation in performance from the removal of the overfitting term c​Nγ/Dδc\,N^{\gamma}/D^{\delta}. The next largest performance degradation comes from tying the N/DN/D term to a single exponent γ\gamma instead of one exponent per parameter. Next, we see slight degradation from removing the saturating wrapper. There is no significant impact from using an exponential wrapper 1−e−h1-e^{-h} instead of our h/(1+h)h/(1+h) wrapper. In the large-scale LLM refits, the difference between our form variants is less pronounced. We observe slight degradation when we remove the overfitting term, but actually observe improvement when we use a single exponent for the N/D{N/D} term. Adding the overfitting term provides extra flexibility that helps the fit surface conform to the true scaling shape, while the shared exponent provides regularization that aids in the identification of the fit parameters when TT and DD are tightly coupled in the training grids.

I.2 Training trajectory plots

The figures below show the empirical running-min validation-loss trajectories across (N,D,C)(N,D,C) cells for each of our four training experiments, decomposed into per-DD and per-NN slices. Figure 2 in the main paper showed a six-cell selection of the MNIST surface; Figure 8 below shows all cells. For CIFAR-100, Darcy, and TinyStories, which use the Warmup-Stable-Decay schedule of §3.1, each cell decomposes into three components: solid lines are the running-min along the stable run, dashed branches are cooldown forks departing from the stable run at log-spaced compute targets, and points mark the final running-min loss at the end of each fork. MNIST uses no LR schedule, so each cell shows a single solid trajectory.

I.3 Held-out prediction plots

Figure 3 in the main paper shows observed-versus-predicted holdout scatter on two representative datasets (Chinchilla and MNIST) under the high-CC holdout. The figures below show the full grid: each of our four training experiments (internal) and each of the five published LLM grids (external), under both the high-CC and high-DD holdouts of §3.1. Rows are datasets, columns are forms; blue points are training cells, orange points are held-out cells. A perfectly calibrated form would place all points on the y=xy=x diagonal.
